title: The History of Scotch Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: From a 1494 tax record to the rules that define Scotch today: how smuggling, the Coffey still and blending made the world's best known whisky.
teaser: Scotch started as farm spirit and smuggled moonshine. Taxes, a new still and some clever blenders turned it global.
standfirst: Scotch whisky has a paper trail going back more than 500 years. Most of what makes it taste the way it does today, from blends to the three year rule, came from a handful of turning points. Here they are in order.
sections: The first written record is a tax entry from 1494

The oldest surviving written reference to Scotch is in the Scottish Exchequer Rolls of 1494. It records eight bolls of malt given to Friar John Cor to make aqua vitae, Latin for water of life. In Gaelic that became uisge beatha, which English speakers shortened to whisky.

For the next few centuries whisky was a farm product. Farmers distilled surplus barley in small pot stills after harvest. The spirit was drunk young and clear, with none of the oak ageing we expect now. It would have tasted closer to raw new make spirit than to anything in a modern bottle.

Once governments noticed whisky, they taxed it. The Scottish parliament put duty on spirits in 1644. After the Union with England in 1707, taxes on malt and spirits rose further. The response in the Highlands was simple: distil in secret. Illicit stills hid in glens. Smugglers moved spirit to towns by pony and boat.

By the early nineteenth century illegal whisky was widely thought to be better than the legal stuff. There was also a lot of it. The Excise Act of 1823 fixed that by making a distilling licence affordable and lowering duty. Within a few years many smugglers had gone legal. Some of the best known distilleries in Speyside date their licences to the years just after the Act.
The column still made blended Scotch possible

In 1830 Aeneas Coffey patented a continuous column still. Unlike a pot still, which is filled, run and emptied in batches, the Coffey still runs non-stop and produces a lighter, stronger spirit from cheaper cereals such as wheat and maize. Our guide on how the Coffey still changed whisky tells that story.

Blenders then discovered that mixing a little heavy malt whisky with a lot of light grain whisky gave a smooth, consistent drink that appealed far beyond Scotland. Changes to the law around 1860 allowed whiskies from different distilleries to be blended under bond, before duty was paid. Blended Scotch was born. The famous blending houses built their brands on it.
A vineyard pest and a crash shaped the industry

In the 1870s and 1880s the phylloxera aphid wiped out vast areas of French vineyards. Cognac grew scarce. British drinkers who had taken brandy and soda moved to whisky and soda instead. We cover it in how phylloxera helped Scotch whisky.

The boom that followed ended badly. Distilleries were built on optimism. In 1898 the collapse of the Pattison blending firm in Leith triggered a crash. Many distilleries closed and the industry spent years recovering. The lesson, that whisky takes years to make and demand can turn in months, still haunts every stock planner.
The three year rule arrived during the First World War

Early in the twentieth century the trade argued about what whisky even was. A Royal Commission reported in 1909 that grain whisky from column stills counted as whisky, not only pot still malt. In 1915 a law required spirit to be aged at least two years before sale. A year later it became three.

That three year minimum survives in today's Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009. Scotch must be distilled and matured in Scotland, in oak casks of no more than 700 litres, for at least three years. It must be bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV. Only water and plain caramel colouring may be added.
The twentieth century brought another boom and bust

After the Second World War, blended Scotch sold strongly around the world, especially in the United States. Distillers expanded and filled casks on the assumption that demand would keep rising. It did not. By the late 1970s and early 1980s tastes had shifted towards lighter spirits such as vodka. Scotland was left with a huge surplus of maturing whisky. The trade called it the whisky loch.

Dozens of distilleries closed or went silent in the early 1980s. Some never reopened. A few of those closed distilleries later became cult names among collectors, precisely because their stock ran out. For anyone working in planning, the story is a reminder that a whisky decision made today is tested by demand ten or twenty years later. We cover that problem in forecasting whisky with long lead times.
Single malt came back into fashion late

For most of the twentieth century almost all Scotch was sold as blends. Bottled single malts were a niche until distillers began promoting them seriously from the 1960s. Today drinkers talk about regions: Speyside, Highland, Lowland, Islay and Campbeltown, each with its own reputation, though style depends more on the distillery than on the map.

The best way to feel this history is to taste a blend and a single malt side by side. Look for the light grain softness in the blend and the heavier cereal, fruit or smoke in the malt. Take small measures with water alongside. Spit if you are tasting several.
faqs: When was Scotch whisky first recorded?
The earliest written record is in the Scottish Exchequer Rolls of 1494, which note malt given to Friar John Cor to make aqua vitae.
How long must Scotch be aged?
At least three years in oak casks in Scotland. The rule dates from 1916 and is now part of the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009.
Why did blended Scotch take off?
The Coffey column still made light grain whisky cheaply. Blending it with malt whisky gave a smoother, consistent drink that sold well far beyond Scotland.
